summary: Registers an ENUM service for H.323, a framework for multimedia communication over packet networks, following the rules in RFC 3761. This lets a phone number point to an H.323 address. It was updated by RFC 6118.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3762 registers one entry type in ENUM, the system that looks up a telephone number in DNS. It matters because a phone number stored in DNS can then point to an H.323 address for voice and video calls.

questions: how does enum work with h.323
how does enum look up an h323 address
what is the h323 uri scheme
subtitle: Registers the E2U+H323 ENUM service so a telephone number can resolve to an H.323 address.

tldr.problem: H.323 multimedia calls on the Internet could use DNS and ENUM to help complete calls, but no ENUM service was registered for H.323.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the service E2U+H323 with the URI scheme h323:, and the ENUM record MUST hold a standard H.323 URL.
tldr.outcome: A telephone number can now resolve to an H.323 URL. The document is a Proposed Standard and RFC 6118 is listed as updating it.

today: RFC 3762 is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 6118 is listed as updating it.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.content:
The H.323 specification defines a means for building multimedia communication services over an arbitrary packet based network, including the Internet. When H.323 is used in the context of the Internet, the RFC notes, it would be useful to take advantage of services such as the domain name system (DNS) and ENUM in order to help facilitate the completion of multimedia calls.

This document registers an ENUM service for H.323 according to the specifications and guidelines in RFC 3761, which defines how a telephone number is looked up in DNS to retrieve a URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone number can be looked up in the internet address book. This RFC adds one kind of answer: the address of an H.323 call system.

sections.title: The Registration Template
sections.content:
Following the template in RFC 3761, the registration gives the service name E2U+H323 and the URI scheme h323:. The functional specification is section 3 of this RFC, the security considerations are section 5, the intended usage is COMMON, the author is Orit Levin, and there is no other information the author deems interesting.

That registration is the only IANA action: the document registers the E2U+H323 ENUM service according to RFC 3761 and the definitions in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration is a short form filled in once: the service is called E2U+H323, its addresses use the h323 scheme, and its normal use is COMMON.

sections.title: The E2U+H323 Service
sections.content:
The service E2U+H323 is used in the service sub-field of the enumservice. The H.323 related ENUM record MUST be populated with a standard H.323 URL as defined in H.323. That URL MAY include parameters specifying the specific protocols and the transport means the H.323 entity supports.

The H.323 entity MUST fully comply with the procedures in RFC 3761 for both record retrieval and processing by the DNS client. If, as a result of the ENUM DNS lookup, an H.323 URL matching local policies and capabilities is retrieved, the procedure defined in section O.8.1 "Locating H.323 Destination" of H.323 Annex O SHOULD be performed.
sections.plainLanguage: The record must contain a proper H.323 address. If it fits what your system can do, you go on with the H.323 steps for finding the destination.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Once the h323-URL information is populated in the DNS it effectively becomes publicly accessible. Access to the H.323 destinations published using ENUM can be secured by techniques and procedures defined in H.235, the security framework for H.323, which defines means for integrity, authentication, non-repudiation and encryption for H.323 calls.

An analysis of threats specific to the dependence of ENUM on the DNS, and the applicability of DNSSEC to these, is provided in RFC 3761.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can read these addresses once they are in DNS, so the call itself has to be protected separately using the H.323 security rules.
